title: Exclusive Time of Functions
description: Brute force to optimized: per-call adjusted start times versus a single shared "previous timestamp" that credits every gap to whoever was actually running.

blocks.text: On a single-threaded CPU, n functions (IDs 0 to n-1) execute, tracked via a call stack: a "start" log pushes a function's ID, an "end" log pops it. Given the logs (each formatted as "id:start_or_end:timestamp"), return the EXCLUSIVE time of each function: the total time it spent running, NOT counting time spent inside any nested (child) function calls.

blocks.caption: A call stack of function IDs directly tracks who is currently executing; time gaps between events are credited to whoever was on top of the stack

blocks.text: Function calls nest like a real call stack: the currently-running function is always whichever ID is on TOP of the stack. Between any two consecutive log events, exactly one function was continuously running (the one on top), so the ELAPSED TIME between those events should be credited entirely to that function, never to whichever function called it.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Relay Race Baton, Timed Precisely
blocks.text: Imagine a relay race where only ONE runner ever holds the baton at a time, and passing it (a nested function call starting) or receiving it back (a nested call finishing) are the only moments that matter. The time between any two such baton-passing moments should be credited entirely to whoever was actually HOLDING the baton during that stretch, never to a runner who had already passed it off.

blocks.caption: A "start" event first credits the time since the last event to whoever was running before pushing the new function; an "end" event credits the final stretch (inclusive) to the function that just finished

blocks.text: Before trying to track each function's total elapsed time and then separately subtracting out nested call durations, notice that tracking the GAP between consecutive log events, and crediting it to whoever was executing during that gap, directly and simply computes exclusive time in a single pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Between any two consecutive log timestamps, exactly ONE function is continuously executing: whichever ID is currently on TOP of the call stack.

Observation 2: When a "start" event occurs, the time elapsed SINCE the previous event was spent by whoever was on top of the stack BEFORE this new function was pushed; that gap should be credited to THEM, not the newly starting function.

Observation 3: When an "end" event occurs, the function being popped was running for the gap since the previous event, PLUS this exact tick itself (since timestamps are INCLUSIVE on both ends); that combined duration is credited to the function now ending.

Observation 4: After crediting an "end" event, the NEXT tracked time should start from immediately AFTER this timestamp (ts + 1), since this exact tick has already been fully accounted for.

Recognizing that credit is always assigned based on WHO WAS ON TOP during a given gap (not based on which function the current log line refers to) is the key insight.

This is a stack-based simulation tracking a "previous timestamp": each log event credits the elapsed gap to whoever was running during that gap (the stack's top before a start, or the function itself on an end), then advances the tracking timestamp accordingly.

Track, for each currently active call, its own running start time; when a call ends, compute its full duration and credit it, then explicitly SUBTRACT that same duration from its caller's running total (since that time was spent nested inside the child, not the caller itself).

items: Maintain a stack of (function ID, adjusted start time) pairs for currently active calls.

When a call ends, compute its full duration (end - start + 1), credit it to that function, and then ADD that same duration to the new top of the stack's tracked start time (effectively shrinking how much time the caller will be credited for, since this nested duration should not count toward it).

codes.python:
def exclusive_time(n, logs):
    result = [0] * n
    running = []                                                            # (function_id, start_timestamp) for every currently-active call
    for log in logs:
        id_str, kind, ts_str = log.split(':')
        fid, ts = int(id_str), int(ts_str)
        if kind == 'start':
            running.append([fid, ts])
        else:
            start_id, start_ts = running.pop()
            duration = ts - start_ts + 1
            result[start_id] += duration
            if running:                                                     # this duration was spent NESTED inside the caller: subtract it back out
                running[-1][1] += duration
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(exclusive_time(2, ["0:start:0", "1:start:2", "1:end:5", "0:end:6"]))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Tracking each call's OWN start time (adjusted as nested children complete) directly computes exclusive duration via subtraction, without needing to track a separate global "previous timestamp."
Adjusting the caller's start time forward by the child's duration is what "removes" the nested time from the caller's eventual total.

blocks.text: Correctly computes exclusive time for every function, since each nested call's duration is explicitly subtracted from its caller's eventual total.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m), where m is the number of logs, each processed once.
Space: O(n), for the call stack (bounded by the maximum nesting depth).

This approach is already close to optimal; the main "optimization" available is simplifying the bookkeeping using a single shared "previous timestamp" variable instead of per-call adjusted start times, which is often considered the cleaner standard solution.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Rather than adjusting each caller's tracked start time as children complete, track a SINGLE shared "previous timestamp" variable globally. On a "start" event, credit the gap since prevTime to whoever is CURRENTLY on top of the stack (before pushing the new function), then update prevTime. On an "end" event, credit the gap since prevTime PLUS this tick itself to the function being popped, then set prevTime to one past this tick.

Maintain a stack of function IDs and a prevTime variable (starting at 0). For a "start" log: if the stack is non-empty, add (ts - prevTime) to the current top's result; push the new function ID; set prevTime = ts. For an "end" log: add (ts - prevTime + 1) to the popped function's result; set prevTime = ts + 1.
Track a single shared "previous timestamp," crediting the gap since it to whoever was running, on every log event.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m), each log processed once.
Space: O(n), for the call stack.

The single prevTime variable always represents "the timestamp up to which time has already been credited to SOMEONE." Every gap since prevTime is credited to exactly one function (whoever was actually executing during that gap), and prevTime is then advanced past whatever was just credited, ensuring no time is ever double-counted or missed. The "+1" on end events correctly accounts for timestamps being INCLUSIVE at both the start and end of a call.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["\"start\" event, stack non-empty","The gap since prevTime is credited to the CURRENT top (about to be superseded by the new nested call)"],["\"start\" event, stack empty","No credit is given (nothing was running before this very first call)"],["\"end\" event","The gap since prevTime, PLUS this final inclusive tick, is credited to the function being popped"]]}

items: Checking "stack is non-empty" before crediting on a start event correctly handles the very first function call, which has no prior running function to credit.
The "+1" adjustment on end events (and the corresponding "ts + 1" for the next prevTime) precisely handles the inclusive timestamp convention this problem uses.
Parsing each log line by splitting on ":" cleanly extracts the function ID, event type, and timestamp for processing.

blocks.text: When a problem literally describes a call stack, modeling it directly with an actual stack (of function IDs) and tracking the gap between consecutive events (crediting it to whoever was executing during that gap) is the natural and efficient approach to computing exclusive time.

items: Forgetting the "+1" adjustment on end events, since timestamps are inclusive on BOTH the start and end of a function call.
Crediting time to the function named in a "start" log line, rather than to whoever was ALREADY running before that new call began.
Mishandling the very first log event (an empty stack), which should not credit any time, since nothing was running before it.

items: Explicitly stating "credit is based on WHO WAS RUNNING during a gap, not which function the current log line names" clarifies the trickiest conceptual point in this problem right away.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "A call stack with start/end events, needing EXCLUSIVE (not total) time per function" points toward tracking the gap between consecutive events, crediting it to whoever was on top of the stack during that gap.

items: How would you compute each function's TOTAL (inclusive of nested calls) time instead? Simply track (end - start + 1) directly per top-level call invocation, without needing to subtract out nested durations at all.

How would this change if timestamps could be non-integer (fractional) values? The same core logic applies directly, just without the "+1" tick adjustment, which specifically exists to handle this problem's inclusive-integer-timestamp convention.

What if logs were NOT guaranteed to be well-formed (mismatched start/end)? Additional validation would be needed, likely rejecting the input or defining explicit error-handling behavior, since the current algorithm assumes well-formed nesting.

A direct, literal application of the call-stack pattern that underlies real program execution, distinct from other stack problems in this category (like Valid Parentheses) in that it tracks accumulated TIME rather than just structural matching.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(m) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (single shared previous-timestamp): O(m) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Call-stack simulation with gap-based time crediting

Core Idea: Track a single "previous timestamp"; every log event credits the elapsed gap since it to whoever was actually running during that gap (the stack's top before a start, or the ending function itself, plus one inclusive tick)
Time: O(m)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Time is always credited based on WHO WAS RUNNING during a gap, never based on which function the current log line happens to name
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: "start": credit gap to current top, then push. "end": credit gap+1 to popped, prevTime=ts+1
